units.title: Unit 49 — Cafés
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 49. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise common drinks and café foods, including those shown in the unit illustrations.
Distinguish British and American meanings of chips, crisps and French fries.
Ask about fillings, sizes and vegetarian options when ordering in a café.
Use natural phrases for eating in, taking away and heating food.
Understand exercise vocabulary and food-and-drink grouping without memorising incidental words.

items.example: I ordered a cappuccino after lunch.
items.note: Coffee made with espresso and hot milk, usually topped with foam.

items.example: She bought a latte on her way to work.
items.note: A coffee drink with plenty of hot milk.

items.example: He prefers black coffee without sugar.
items.note: Coffee served without milk; black describes how it is served.

items.example: I had hot chocolate because I didn't want coffee.
items.note: A hot drink made with chocolate or cocoa and milk or water.

items.example: The children ordered strawberry milkshakes.
items.note: A cold, sweet drink made by mixing milk with another flavour.

items.example: I usually drink herbal tea before bed.
items.note: A drink made by putting herbs or other plants in hot water.

items.example: Do you have decaf tea for the evening?
items.note: Tea with most or all of its caffeine removed.

items.example: Could I have a decaf coffee, please?
items.note: Coffee with most or all of its caffeine removed.

items.example: She made a smoothie with bananas and berries.
items.note: A thick, usually cold drink made by blending fruit or vegetables.

items.example: I asked for decaf because it was getting late.
items.note: Short for decaffeinated; contrasts with a drink containing caffeine. The book shows decaf tea and coffee.

items.example: I had a warm waffle with fruit for breakfast.
items.note: A baked cake-like food with a pattern of small squares.

items.example: I'd like a cheese toastie, please.
items.note: British English: a hot toasted sandwich, often with melted cheese.

items.example: The café serves a chicken panini with salad.
items.note: A sandwich made with Italian-style bread, usually pressed or toasted.

items.pt: bagel; pão em formato de anel
items.example: I bought a bagel with cream cheese.
items.note: A round bread roll with a hole in the middle.

items.pt: wrap; sanduíche enrolado em pão fino
items.example: She ordered a vegetable wrap for lunch.
items.note: A thin piece of bread rolled round a filling.

items.pt: batatas chips; batatas fritas de pacote
items.example: He bought a packet of crisps to eat with his sandwich.
items.note: British English: very thin fried potato slices sold in packets; called chips in American English.

items.example: We shared a baguette filled with cheese.
items.note: A long, narrow loaf of bread, sometimes used for sandwiches.

items.example: She chose a blueberry muffin with her tea.
items.note: A small individual cake, often sweet, as shown in the unit.

items.example: There were colourful cupcakes in the display.
items.note: A small cake for one person, often with icing on top.

items.example: I usually have a croissant and coffee for breakfast.
items.note: A light, flaky, crescent-shaped pastry.

items.pt: batatas fritas em palitos, geralmente mais grossos
items.example: We had fish and chips by the sea.
items.note: In British English, chips are fried potato sticks served hot; in the US these are often called fries.

items.example: She opened a bag of chips at the picnic.
items.note: In American English, chips are thin, crispy fried potato slices; called crisps in the UK.

items.example: I'd like a sandwich with fries on the side.
items.note: Also called French fries; an alternative to chips for fried potato sticks.

items.example: The children ordered French fries with their lunch.
items.note: The American name for what is often called chips in the UK.

items.example: A regular coffee will be fine, thanks.
items.note: A standard size at the café, contrasted with large; its exact volume can vary.

items.example: Could I have a large hot chocolate?
items.note: A bigger serving size than regular.

items.example: Is that to have in or take away?
items.note: Used when ordering food or drink to consume inside the café.

items.example: I'd like this coffee to take away, please.
items.note: British English: food or drink ordered to consume after leaving the café; contrasts with to have in.

items.example: Do you have a vegetarian sandwich?
items.note: Food suitable for someone who does not eat meat or fish.

items.example: Could you heat the panini up for me?
items.note: Make food warm or hot, often using an oven or microwave. Separable: heat it up, not heat up it.

items.example: There are clean napkins next to the till.
items.note: Pieces of paper used to wipe your mouth and fingers while eating.

items.example: She carried the drinks to the table on a tray.
items.note: A flat object used to carry several drinks or food items.

items.pt: O que tem nesse panini?; qual é o recheio?
items.example: I asked the assistant what was in the sandwich.
items.note: A natural question when you want to know the ingredients or filling.

items.word: I'll have one of those, please.
items.pt: Vou querer um desses, por favor.
items.example: I'll have one of those, please, and a drink.
items.note: A polite phrase to choose an item just mentioned or shown; I'll have is a common way to order.

items.example: The cashier said, 'Here you go,' as she handed me the tray.
items.note: An informal, friendly expression used when handing something to another person.

items.pt: misto quente de queijo e tomate
items.example: I ordered a cheese and tomato toastie for lunch.
items.note: A common toasted-sandwich filling combination used in the practice activities.

items.example: Can I also have a chocolate muffin?
items.note: A natural noun-noun combination for a flavoured muffin.

items.example: Is the sandwich to eat in or take away?
items.note: Alternative to to have in; introduced in the unit's practice dialogue.

items.example: A latte, please, and a bottle of water.
items.note: A brief, polite pattern for ordering a drink; the noun can be changed.

sectionsChecked: A: Drinks; illustrated drink types, decaf distinction
B: Food; food illustrations and UK–US comparison of crisps and chips
C: Ordering food and drink; café dialogues, sizes, eating in/taking away, fillings and serving items
Exercises 49.1–49.5; categories, vocabulary contrasts, sentence matching, dialogue and personal practice

units.title: Unit 50 — Sightseeing holidays
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 50. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Identify common tourist landmarks and distinguish religious buildings from other sights.
Describe sightseeing activities using natural verb and noun combinations.
Talk about exploring, getting lost, going out and buying souvenirs.
Describe places as magnificent, lively or packed, and identify their main attractions.
Recommend experiences correctly with worth + noun or worth + -ing.

items.example: We visited the old royal palace on Saturday.
items.note: A large, impressive building where a king, queen or other important person lives or lived.

items.example: We bought fresh fruit at the street market.
items.note: A place where people buy and sell goods, often from stalls.

items.example: The castle stands on a hill above the village.
items.note: A large, strong old building, often built for defence.

items.example: We took photos beside a beautiful fountain.
items.note: A structure that sends water into the air, often in a square or garden.

items.example: The mosque has an impressive central dome.
items.note: A building where Muslims worship.

items.example: Visitors can see the stained-glass windows in the cathedral.
items.note: An important Christian church, usually the main church of a bishop's area.

items.example: They visited an ancient temple during their trip.
items.note: A building used for worship in several religions.

items.example: A stone statue stands in the centre of the square.
items.note: A sculpture of a person or animal, usually made of stone or metal.

items.example: The village church is open to visitors in the afternoon.
items.note: A Christian place of worship; included in the exercise on religious buildings.

items.pt: passear para conhecer pontos turísticos; fazer turismo
items.example: We went sightseeing after breakfast.
items.note: Go around visiting interesting or famous places.

items.example: We had two days to see the sights.
items.note: Visit the main attractions of a place; a synonym of go sightseeing.

items.example: They did a lot of sightseeing in their first week.
items.note: Use do with sightseeing to talk about how much sightseeing you do.

items.pt: fazer um pouco de turismo; alguns passeios
items.example: Let's do a bit of sightseeing before lunch.
items.note: A smaller amount of tourist visiting than do a lot of sightseeing.

items.pt: dar uma olhada; passear para conhecer o local
items.example: We had a look round the museum before lunch.
items.note: Visit or explore a place casually, often on foot; round is common in British English.

items.pt: sair para passear ou se divertir
items.example: We went out for dinner most evenings.
items.note: Leave your accommodation for a social activity, such as eating at a restaurant.

items.example: We got lost in the narrow streets.
items.note: Lose your way; the past form is got lost.

items.example: We had a great time exploring the city.
items.note: Enjoy an experience very much; past: had a great time.

items.example: I hope you have a nice time on holiday.
items.note: Have a pleasant experience; can also be used as a friendly wish.

items.example: They had a terrible time because it rained all week.
items.note: Have a very unpleasant experience; the opposite of having a great time.

items.example: We bought souvenirs for our friends at home.
items.note: Buy objects to help you remember a place or experience.

items.example: Sightseeing is easier when the weather is good.
items.note: The activity of visiting interesting places, especially on holiday.

items.example: We explored a quiet neighbourhood on foot.
items.note: Travel or walk around an unfamiliar place to discover what is there.

items.example: I kept the ticket as a souvenir of our trip.
items.note: Something bought or kept to remind you of a place or event.

items.pt: explorar; percorrer um mercado ou feira
items.example: We explored the market and tried some local food.
items.note: Explore can be followed directly by a place; no preposition is needed.

items.example: It's a lovely place to spend a weekend.
items.note: A general word that can describe a building, area, town or country depending on context.

items.example: We bought a guidebook before travelling.
items.note: A book containing practical information about places to visit.

items.example: The view from the top of the hill was magnificent.
items.note: Extremely impressive, beautiful or excellent.

items.example: The museum was packed on Saturday afternoon.
items.note: Very crowded, with too many people in a place.

items.example: The town centre is lively at night.
items.note: Full of activity and energy; often positive when describing places.

items.example: There is plenty of food for everyone.
items.note: A large amount or more than enough of something; often followed by of.

items.example: The old bridge is an important historic site.
items.note: Important or significant in history; often used with monuments and sites.

items.example: A monument in the square remembers the city's history.
items.note: An important or commemorative structure, often associated with the past.

items.example: The castle is the town's main attraction.
items.note: A place or feature that interests visitors and brings people there.

items.pt: que vale a pena; de valor
items.example: The museum is worth the entrance fee.
items.note: Worth is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not a to-infinitive, in this pattern.

items.example: The square was packed with tourists at midday.
items.note: Use packed with to identify the people filling a place.

items.example: There's plenty to do near the harbour.
items.note: Indicates many available activities, especially in a lively place.

items.example: The city has many historic monuments to visit.
items.note: Important structures associated with earlier periods of history.

items.example: The main attraction was the enormous palace.
items.note: The most important or popular reason for visiting a place.

items.example: The cathedral is definitely worth visiting.
items.note: Use worth + -ing to recommend an activity; not worth to visit.

items.example: The evening light show is worth seeing.
items.note: Worth + -ing suggests that the experience is a good idea.

items.pt: vale uma visita; vale a pena conhecer
items.example: The local market is worth a visit.
items.note: Worth + noun is an alternative to worth visiting.

items.example: We visited several tourist attractions in the old town.
items.note: Places visitors especially want to see; also appears in the practice activities.

items.pt: olhar ao redor; conhecer o local
items.example: We looked round the old shops before leaving.
items.note: A shorter form related to have a look round; can refer to visiting or inspecting a place.

sectionsChecked: A: Things to see; labelled photographs of landmarks and religious buildings
B: Tourist activities; activities table and usage examples
C: Describing places; guidebooks, crowded and lively places, monuments and worth patterns
Exercises 50.1–50.4; identifying religious places, email gaps, paraphrases and personal practice
